text: Redis's object header (redisObject) holds type:4, encoding:4 and a 24-bit lru field (LRU_BITS = 24), then a refcount and a pointer to the value. Under LFU the same 24 bits hold a 16-bit access time and an 8-bit frequency counter.
why: Gives the exact layout behind the '4 + 28 bits' figure.

text: Redis approximates LRU. At eviction time it samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5), evicts the one idle longest, and since Redis 3.0 keeps a pool of good candidates. With 10 samples the result is very close to true LRU.
why: Shows LRU is doable under tight memory without a linked list.

text: Redis LFU uses a probabilistic logarithmic (Morris) counter that saturates around one million hits and decays over time. lfu-log-factor (default 10) and lfu-decay-time (default 1 minute) tune it.
why: Explains how frequency fits in 8 bits and why old popularity fades.

text: In Redis, maxmemory 0 (the default on 64-bit) means no limit. Replication and AOF buffers are not counted toward maxmemory, so leave some RAM free for them.
why: Practical detail when setting the cap.

text: Redis eviction policies: noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-lru, volatile-lfu, volatile-random, volatile-ttl, and since Redis 8.6 allkeys-lrm/volatile-lrm. The volatile-* policies only consider keys with a TTL.
why: Complete, current list of policies.

text: Current Redis (expire.c) walks the table of keys with a TTL incrementally with a cursor, 20 keys per loop. It keeps going while more than about 10% of checked keys are expired (tunable with active-expire-effort), within a CPU budget.
why: Updates the classic 20-keys/25% description.

text: Redis keeps a separate index of keys that have a TTL (db->expires). The active expiry cycle scans it, and Redis docs note that setting an expire costs memory.
why: TTL handling still needs some extra structure, just not a priority queue.

text: HTTP/1.1 defaults to persistent connections (RFC 9112 §9.3), so one TCP connection serves many requests. Closing a TCP connection takes a FIN and an ACK in each direction.
why: Corrects the connection-per-request picture of HTTP/1.1.

text: A valid HTTP/1.1 request must include a Host header, and the headers end with an empty line (CRLF CRLF). A strict server answers 400 Bad Request if Host is missing.
why: Lets readers reproduce the netcat experiment against any server.

text:
RESP sends commands as arrays of length-prefixed bulk strings (e.g. *2
$4
LLEN
$6
mylist
), so it is binary-safe and fast to parse. Redis also accepts plain 'inline' commands typed in telnet, the same trick as the netcat HTTP demo.
why: Concrete picture of a custom protocol.

text: gRPC frames each message with a 1-byte compressed flag and a 4-byte length over HTTP/2. Message compression is only used when a grpc-encoding header is set.
why: Clarifies where gRPC's efficiency comes from.

text: Redis is 'mostly single threaded': commands run on one main thread, while background threads do work such as UNLINK lazy-free, and optional I/O threads handle socket reads, writes and parsing.
why: Current state of Redis threading.

text: In Redis Cluster a node that does not own a key's hash slot replies with a redirect such as '-MOVED 3999 127.0.0.1:6381', and the client retries at that address.
why: Shows Redis's actual redirect mechanism.

text: Redis Cluster does not use a consistent-hashing ring. It maps keys to 16384 hash slots with HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384 and assigns slots to master nodes, moving whole slots when resharding.
why: A widely used alternative to the ring for ownership.

text: Amazon's Dynamo paper uses virtual nodes so that a failed node's load 'is evenly dispersed across the remaining available nodes', and a new node takes roughly equal load from each existing node.
why: The other side of the virtual-node trade-off.

text: Cassandra's docs list the cost of many tokens per node: more neighbours per token range, a higher probability of an outage, and more repair operations. Since 3.x a deterministic allocator gives balance with far fewer tokens than the old default of 256.
why: Balanced view of operational cost of vnodes.

text: In Dynamo each key is stored on N nodes: the coordinator and its N-1 clockwise successors on the ring. Cassandra's replication factor likewise counts total copies (RF=3 means three replicas).
why: Fixes the replication-factor counting convention.

text: Redis AOF is off by default (RDB snapshots are the default). With the default 'appendfsync everysec' you can lose about one second of writes; 'always' fsyncs on every write but is very slow.
why: Durability depends on fsync policy.

text: In BitTorrent's Kademlia DHT a node asks the nodes it knows closest to the target. They return either peers or even closer nodes, and the requester 'iteratively queries nodes that are closer' until none are closer.
why: Concrete DHT routing behaviour.

text: Memcached keeps a doubly linked LRU list per slab class, split into HOT, WARM and COLD sub-lists. Production caches do pay for linked-list LRU when they judge it worth it.
why: Counter-example to 'real caches avoid linked lists'.

text: MySQL's InnoDB buffer pool makes LRU scan-resistant with midpoint insertion: new pages enter at the head of an 'old' sublist (3/8 of the pool by default) and are promoted only if accessed again.
why: Another way to solve the scan problem without LFU.

text: InnoDB lock compatibility: if T1 holds a shared (S) lock on a row, T2 can also get S, but T2's exclusive (X) request must wait. Two transactions that both hold S and both try to update deadlock, and InnoDB rolls one back.
why: Explains what actually happens with shared locks.

text: In InnoDB, a REPEATABLE READ snapshot applies to SELECT, not necessarily to UPDATE/DELETE. DML can affect rows another transaction just committed, so check the condition in the UPDATE itself (e.g. WHERE seat_free = 1).
why: Practical fix for double-booking.

text: MySQL closes non-interactive connections idle longer than wait_timeout (default 28800 seconds), so connection pools validate or refresh idle connections.
why: Real-world caveat for writing your own pool.

text: Linux overcommits memory by default, so malloc can succeed without physical memory behind it. If the system later runs out, 'one or more processes will be killed by the OOM killer'.
why: Explains what really ends a memory-hungry program on Linux.
